who participated in a protest Friday.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Anthony Vazquez/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Lillian is worried about the financial cost, too. The 17-year-old would rather the U.S. put <a class="Link" href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/03/11/world/middleeast/iran-war-costs-pentagon.html" target="_blank" ><u>the billions it has spent on the war with Iran</u></a> toward other causes, like education, health care or improving infrastructure.</p><p>“There’s so many better things to put that money towards than war,” Lillian said. “My friends and I will talk about it outside of school, and it's a pressing issue to all of us.”</p><p>More than 1,900 people in Iran and nearly 1,100 people in Lebanon have been killed in the war. Millions have been displaced. Eighteen people have died in Israel, while four Israeli soldiers have also been killed in Lebanon. Thirteen U.S. military members have died.</p><p>“We’re all just scared of the death and the destruction that the major war powers are enacting, and it’s ridiculous, quite frankly,” said Kevin Watts, a junior. “I think the students here know that and they are fighting against it with this and with other protests.”</p><p>Kevin, a member of the school’s student union, which organized the protest, said while students are discussing these issues amongst each other in and out of school, the rally was also intended to raise awareness among those who aren’t as plugged in.</p><p>“People are definitely aware of what’s happening with immigration. They're aware about the war. Many of our students drive so they’re aware that the gas prices are going up,” Kevin said. “Some of them may be wondering why, which is why we have things like this.”</p><div class="Enhancement" title: CPS Board selects Macquline King as permanent CEO, will vote on her contract Monday
author: Emmanuel Camarillo
summary: <p>The Chicago Board of Education will vote on Monday to appoint Macquline King as the permanent leader of Chicago Public Schools, catapulting a Black woman with homegrown talent to the district’s top post 10 months after she was appointed to the interim role.</p><p>According to <a class="Link" href="https://www.cpsboe.org/content/documents/march_30_2026_special_board_meeting_public_agenda_to_post.pdf" target="_blank" ><u>documents posted on the CPS Board’s website</u></a> Thursday, the school board has offered King the job and she has accepted it.</p><p>The proposed contract would be effective July 1 through June 30, 2029 — meaning she would lead the district well past the transition to a fully elected school board. If approved, King’s salary will start at $380,000, more than former CEO Pedro Martinez was offered. He was granted a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/education/2021/10/25/22744850/cps-ceo-pedro-martinez-salary-contract-public-school#:~:text=CPS%20CEO%20Pedro%20Martinez%20to,year%20contract%20%2D%20Chicago%20Sun%2DTimes" target="_blank" ><u>$340,000 annual salary on a five-year contract.</u></a></p><p>This brings to the end a <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/2026/03/13/cps-board-names-3-finalists-to-lead-district-interim-ceo-king-former-nyc-east-baton-rouge-schools-chiefs" target="_blank" ><u>protracted search</u></a> for a new leader of the school district. It started last year after <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/2024/12/20/cps-ceo-pedro-martinez-threatens-to-sue-school-board-before-they-consider-firing-him-at-friday-meeting" target="_blank" ><u>Martinez was fired</u></a>.</p><p>Though the contract appoints her as CEO, King has a superintendent’s license, which the partly elected, partly appointed board <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/2025/03/20/cps-school-board-votes-to-require-next-leader-be-an-educator-not-a-ceo" target="_blank" ><u>made a requirement for the position</u></a>. Those who have worked with King say she is an expert on teaching and learning, as well as building relationships and cultivating leadership.</p><p>Unlike some past CPS leaders, she does not have a background in accounting and will likely have to find a strong chief financial officer to help her navigate the district’s budget and debt. CPS is projected to face a $500 million deficit next school year, as well as future deficits.</p><p>King started as a teacher in CPS and became a principal of Dumas Elementary School on the South Side in 2007. She served there until CPS closed the school in 2013. She then became principal of a North Side elementary, which took in students from a nearby closed school.</p><p>She applied for the CEO position in 2021, but was passed over for Martinez. Mayor Lori Lightfoot hired King in 2022 to work in her office as the deputy education mayor.</p><p>Brandon Johnson kept King on when he became mayor. One of Johnson’s former top officials, who did not want to be named because they were not authorized to speak on the matter, called King a “wonderful person who was really well-liked.”</p><p>Though the school board is partially elected, Johnson still appoints the majority of its members.</p><p>As interim CEO, King immediately had to confront a budget deficit that <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/2025/06/26/interim-chicago-public-schools-ceo-pegs-deficit-at-730-million" target="_blank" ><u>she pegged at more than $700 million</u></a>. She gained the respect of some of Johnson’s opponents by <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/2025/08/14/majority-of-cps-board-demands-a-budget-with-pension-payment-and-loan-rebuffing-proposal-from-cps-leaders" target="_blank" ><u>refusing to present a budget</u></a> that included borrowing, which was something that the mayor’s office argued the budget should allow for.</p><p>King <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/education/2025/11/05/cps-ceo-search-macquline-king" target="_blank" ><u>wasn’t among the finalists in the fall</u></a>, which became a point of contention among some groups who supported her, such as the Westside Branch of the NAACP. But her standing among board members has risen over the last few months as she’s handled <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-school-board/2025/08/28/cps-board-denies-johnsons-preferred-budget-rejects-pension-payment-and-loan" target="_blank" ><u>tense budget discussions,</u></a> the closings of <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/education/2026/03/19/cps-revokes-aspiras-ability-to-operate-charter-schools-in-chicago-in-rare-move-board-of-education" target="_blank" ><u>privately managed public schools</u></a> and widespread <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/education/2026/02/12/no-recess-lockdowns-less-learning-how-immigration-agents-disrupted-cps-schools-this-fall" target="_blank" ><u>immigration enforcement that affected schools.</u></a> Board member Jitu Brown has said serving in the interim post has been like an “on the job interview” for King.</p><p>The board named three finalists earlier this month, but one of the candidates, Meisha Porter, the former leader of New York City’s school system, dropped out without offering a reason days later.</p><p>The other finalist was Sito Narcisse, the former head of Louisiana's second-largest school district, whose past job experience was somewhat polarizing. <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/education/2026/03/24/finalist-for-cps-ceo-sito-narcisse-courted-controversy-in-past-jobs-but-defenders-praise-his-vision" target="_blank" ><u>Some praised him as a “transformational leader”</u></a> but others criticized his leadership style.</p><p>There were some concerns among community members that the <a class="Link" href="https://www.chalkbeat.org/chicago/2026/03/18/chicago-public-schools-lacks-latino-ceo-finalists/" target="_blank" ><u>finalists didn’t include a Latino candidate</u></a>. Chalkbeat Chicago reported that a fourth finalist dropped out, but board members wouldn’t say if that person was Latino.</p>

title: Finalist for CPS CEO courted controversy in past jobs, but defenders praise his bold vision
author: Emmanuel Camarillo
summary: <p>When Meisha Porter, the former leader of New York City’s school system, withdrew her name from consideration to become the CEO of Chicago Public Schools last week, the district suddenly found itself with just two candidates for the job.</p><p>One of them is Macquline King, who has been serving as CPS’ interim leader since June. The former CPS principal did not make the cut to be a finalist back in the fall. But some board members have recently warmed up to her, citing how she’s handled contentious issues, such as <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/2025/08/14/majority-of-cps-board-demands-a-budget-with-pension-payment-and-loan-rebuffing-proposal-from-cps-leaders" target="_blank" ><u>the budget process</u></a> and <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/education/2026/02/12/no-recess-lockdowns-less-learning-how-immigration-agents-disrupted-cps-schools-this-fall" target="_blank" ><u>responding to aggressive immigration enforcement</u></a> that impacted schools.</p><p>Given the <a class="Link" href="https://www.chalkbeat.org/chicago/2026/03/20/meisha-porter-withdraws-from-chicago-public-schools-ceo-search/" target="_blank" ><u>dwindling field</u></a> and <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/2026/03/13/cps-board-names-3-finalists-to-lead-district-interim-ceo-king-former-nyc-east-baton-rouge-schools-chiefs" target="_blank" ><u>protracted search</u></a>, King’s standing appears to be rising.</p><p>The other is Sito Narcisse, a former leader of Louisiana’s second-largest school district who has been linked to controversies in his previous roles, leading some to question how he made it to be a finalist to lead the third-largest school district in the country with many red flags.</p><p>His work at times has been polarizing. In Baton Rouge, families sued him and the district over a controversial event he promoted. Early in his career in Boston, Narcisse was criticized for making sweeping changes at the school he led with little or no community input, a concern that would follow him.</p><p>Supporters say Narcisse has been a victim of local politics that have stymied his vision, calling him a “transformational leader” who moves fast to drive change and increase positive outcomes for students.</p><p>For his part, Narcisse says that while not everyone has supported all his moves, he’s made decisions with the best interests of students in mind.</p><p>“In every place I have been, outcomes for students and culture for staff have improved,” Narcisse wrote in an email to the Sun-Times/WBEZ.</p><h3>Lawsuit and ties to ousted leader </h3><p>One of the most notable controversies happened when Narcisse was superintendent of Louisiana’s East Baton Rouge Parish Schools, which he led from 2021 to 2024. It was the only time he’s served as the top leader of a school district.</p><p>Families filed a lawsuit against Narcisse and the school board in 2023 <a class="Link" href="https://www.theadvocate.com/baton_rouge/news/education/parents-students-complain-east-baton-rouge-schools-field-trip-was-more-like-church-service/article_97dc38c2-3a0d-11ed-a388-3f7b65892ceb.html" target="_blank" ><u>alleging the district misled parents </u></a>when it promoted a career fair for seniors hosted at a local church that included overt religious messaging.</p><p>The families allege that organizers split high schoolers into groups by gender and had the boys compete in physical contests while girls were “graphically lectured by pastors and other religious figures about virginity, rape, abuse, and suicide and were told to ‘forgive’ their rapists and abusers,” according to the lawsuit.</p><p>Narcisse <a class="Link" href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=93PB0iA_Uiw&t=116s" target="_blank" ><u>appeared on local television</u></a> to promote the “Day of Hope” alongside one of the co-founders of the organizers, 29:11 Academy, whose name is a reference to the Bible, <a class="Link" href="https://www.2911mentor.com/" target="_blank" ><u>according to its website</u></a>. They talked about how the event could help students find careers and make good choices, but didn’t mention any religious components.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://www.theadvocate.com/baton_rouge/news/education/judge-keeps-baton-rouge-school-board-in-day-of-hope-suit/article_397de226-8b23-11ef-8a4e-432f40734807.html" target="_blank" ><u>Board members have said</u> t</a>hat they were out of the loop because the district allows the superintendent to award contracts worth less than $10,000 without board approval. <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbrz.com/news/day-of-hope-cost-school-system-only-200-less-than-amount-required-for-school-board-approval/" target="_blank" ><u>This contract totaled $9,800.</u></a></p><p>Narcisse has denied the allegations in the lawsuit, which is ongoing, and the case is heading to a possible trial, according to court records.</p><p>In response to questions about the event, Narcisse wrote in an email that the “Day of Hope” was established 10 years before he became superintendent and he was “not aware of any religious components.” He said “the focus was on motivating students to stay in school, explore their futures, and think about next steps.”</p><p>Michael Gaudet, who was on the East Baton Rouge school board at the time, and is still a member, defended Narcisse, saying the situation was “drummed up” by an attorney “who is a publicity hound.” <a class="Link" href="https://www.theadvocate.com/baton_rouge/news/education/participants-defend-controversial-day-of-hope-event-to-school-board-we-all-enjoyed-it/article_e3fd0e5a-45b8-11ed-bc0d-c7a6b674f638.html" target="_blank" ><u>Some participants said they enjoyed the event.</u></a></p><p>“We could have probably done a better job of monitoring that, but none of the allegations have ever been proven true,” Gaudet said.</p><p>He pointed to the school board’s <a class="Link" href="https://www.theadvocate.com/baton_rouge/news/education/no-evidence-for-day-of-hope-controversy-school-leader-says-board-could-seek-investigation/article_c20ac41a-45b6-11ed-9962-4f58e489f0d1.html" target="_blank" ><u>internal investigation</u></a> which “found no evidential proof” of the claims, though several students and parents spoke to local news outlets to express concerns. Some board members introduced a resolution calling for an independent investigation, but <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbrz.com/news/ebr-schools-superintendent-says-criticism-of-day-of-hope-has-been-unfair/" target="_blank" ><u>that was voted down</u></a>.</p><p>Gaudet said the situation was like “a tempest in a teapot… There was nothing to it.”</p><p>In 2023 the school board <a class="Link" href="https://www.theadvocate.com/baton_rouge/news/education/narcisse-rejected-next-baton-rouge-schools-leader-unclear/article_afc3b158-9539-11ee-84e6-bb9fa648edc7.html" target="_blank" ><u>narrowly voted not to renew Narcisse’s contract</u></a> amid a debate about a pay raise. He agreed to a voluntary buyout and stepped down after three years in charge. <a class="Link" href="https://www.theadvocate.com/baton_rouge/news/education/narcisse-supporters-rally-to-keep-baton-rouge-schools-chief/article_d7191668-9dee-11ee-bc28-0b3178838957.html" target="_blank" ><u>A group of supporters rallied to keep him. </u></a></p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-floatLeft> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-a00000" class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Michael Gaudet, a school board member in East Baton Rouge Parish, says his school district parted ways with Narcisse for reasons unrelated to performance.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>East Baton Rouge Parish School Board</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Gaudet said the decision not to renew Narcisse’s contract wasn’t due to his performance. He said that six new board members were voted onto the nine-member body during Narcisse’s tenure, and most wanted to move in a different direction.</p><p>A few years earlier, Narcisse faced a turbulent tenure as the chief of schools at Metro Nashville Public Schools, where he was second-in-command to director of schools Shawn Joseph. Joseph hired Narcisse after the two worked together at Prince George’s County Public Schools in suburban Maryland.</p><p>Joseph’s three-year tenure in Nashville was <a class="Link" href="https://www.newschannel5.com/news/newschannel-5-investigates/what-you-need-to-know-about-shawn-josephs-controversies" target="_blank" ><u>marked by a string of controversies</u></a>, including claims that he mishandled allegations of sexual harassment against a principal and complaints that he attempted to award no-bid contracts. A veteran administrator also accused the district of pay discrimination between men and women in high-level positions and said Narcisse, her boss at the time, <a class="Link" href="https://www.newschannel5.com/news/newschannel-5-investigates/metro-schools/administrator-accuses-mnps-of-pay-discrimination-retaliation" target="_blank" ><u>questioned her performance</u></a> when she dug into the district’s salary data.</p><p>In response to questions from the Sun-Times/WBEZ, Narcisse said he did not make salary decisions when he worked in Nashville.</p><p>The board eventually <a class="Link" href="https://wpln.org/post/shawn-josephs-contract-is-terminated-during-heated-school-board-meeting/" target="_blank" ><u>decided to buy out Joseph’s contract.</u></a> Narcisse voluntarily left the district shortly after.</p><p>Amy Frogge, who was on the school board in Nashville at the time and was among Joseph’s most outspoken critics, said that while Joseph was the face of the controversies, Narcisse likely knew what the superintendent was up to as his No. 2.</p><p>"They were extremely close, they were friends,” Frogge said. "It was a painful few years in Nashville when they were there.”</p><h3>Some bristle at leadership style, while others celebrate it</h3><p>Some teachers and former school board members who worked alongside Narcisse have criticized his leadership style, saying he has a bold vision for education but has sometimes overlooked community concerns.</p><p>Dawn Chanet Collins, who served on the East Baton Rouge Parish School Board when Narcisse was superintendent, said his ideas sometimes clashed with those of longtime staff and community members who felt he needed to better understand the makeup of the district before making changes.</p><p>“Each instance where he made decisions that resulted in public chaos he was advised otherwise by staff who would explain the possible consequences of various decisions,” said Collins, who was often vocal when she disagreed with his decisions. “He appeared to not either hear or not care about the potential issues that were being raised.”</p><p>For example, when Narcisse wanted to equitably deal with staffing shortages ahead of the 2022-2023 school year, he <a class="Link" href="https://www.theadvocate.com/baton_rouge/news/education/as-parents-teachers-protest-baton-rouge-school-re-staffing-school-board-seeks-explanation/article_a1886f92-d619-11ec-b975-874bd1939115.html" target="_blank" ><u>decided to reassign teachers and other staff</u></a> to schools that were understaffed. Hundreds of employees were told their positions were eliminated and they could apply for the vacant positions at other schools or be reassigned.</p><p>It’s the kind of shakeup that would be hard to pull off without criticism. <a class="Link" href="https://www.theadvocate.com/baton_rouge/news/education/superintendent-faces-protest-loads-of-questions-on-re-staffing-of-baton-rouge-schools/article_7509cdf4-d7a8-11ec-aa1e-ab8f10afd905.html" target="_blank" ><u>Some community members supported the initiative</u></a>, saying those speaking out against it mostly came from schools that already had plenty of resources.</p><p>But employees who were happy with their roles were upset, saying it disrupted school communities and programs and took away principal autonomy. Parents protested at board meetings. Several board members criticized Narcisse for not working with them on the changes. One said his <a class="Link" href="https://www.theadvocate.com/baton_rouge/news/education/superintendent-faces-protest-loads-of-questions-on-re-staffing-of-baton-rouge-schools/article_7509cdf4-d7a8-11ec-aa1e-ab8f10afd905.html" target="_blank" ><u>top-down management was “breeding mistrust.”</u></a></p><p>Narcisse’s supporters say his initiatives focus on what’s best for students and the pushback stems from resistance to altering the status quo.</p><p>“When you talk about change, that can sometimes be uncomfortable but it’s for the better good of students,” said Dadrius Lanus, who served as school board president in East Baton Rouge Parish when Narcisse was superintendent and is still on the board.</p><p>“Every superintendent is going to have some pushback from the community, but the question is, the moves that he was able to make, did it better our district? And I would say absolutely,” Lanus said.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-floatLeft> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-ac0000" to Bright Futures” program</u></a> that Narcisse spearheaded as an example. The program helps high schoolers earn college credits or career credentials. Lanus also said Narcisse was responsible for expanding kindergarten access in the district, among other accomplishments.</p><p>But to Ursula Parkerson, a teacher in East Baton Rouge Parish, Narcisse “came in like a wrecking ball” and pushed forward with his plans despite concerns from the community. That dynamic led to low morale among educators, said Parkerson, a member of the East Baton Rouge Parish Association of Educators, a local teachers union.</p><p>“He was wanting to make big changes and not really caring, it felt like to us, about who got railroaded in the process,” Parkerson said.</p><p>Narcisse faced similar criticisms early in his career, too. As the leader of a struggling public high school in Boston, he tried several controversial turnaround strategies including eliminating the grade “D,” establishing single-sex classrooms and getting rid of many staffers. Three-quarters of the school’s teachers and administrators left, <a class="Link" href="https://web.archive.org/web/20141017071730/https://www.bostonglobe.com/metro/2012/06/24/troubled-english-high-school-showing-little-improvement-after-three-tumultuous-years-under-untested-headmaster-sito-narcisse/XNwPoz4RLD02uCdWePvEfK/story.html" target="_blank" ><u>according to The Boston Globe</u></a>, and while test scores ticked up slightly, the dropout rate, failure rate and absentee rate all rose, as well.</p><p>Gaudet pushed back on critics who said Narcisse didn’t take input from others into account, though he conceded that Narcisse might have moved too quickly at times in Baton Rouge.</p><p>“I would say his philosophy towards leadership is always what’s best for the kids and his leadership style is very collaborative,” Gaudet said. “I think maybe he tried to do a little too much too fast, but it was in a desire to move the needle.”</p><p>Lanus said he wished East Baton Rouge Parish had kept Narcisse on.</p><p>“If Chicago Public Schools were to select him, they are literally selecting somebody who can take the district to the next level,” Lanus said. “They’re going to get a transformational leader.”</p>

title: Leaders at Southwest Side elementary school named for Cesar Chavez moving to potentially rename school
author: Sun-Times staff
summary: <p>Leaders at a Chicago public school named after Cesar Chavez, who co-founded the United Farm Workers, have started a process that could change the school’s name. </p><p>This comes after <a class="Link" href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/03/18/us/cesar-chavez-sexual-abuse-allegations-ufw.html" target="_blank" >a New York Times investigation published Wednesday</a> found that Chavez groomed young girls who worked in the movement. Chicago Public Schools officials say leaders at Cesar E. Chavez Multicultural Academic Center in the Back of the Yards neighborhood have begun getting community feedback. Any recommendation would have to go to the Local School Council and ultimately the school board. </p><p>Chavez, who died in 1993, has long been lionized in Chicago’s Latino and labor strongholds. <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago/2026/03/18/allegations-of-abuse-by-cesar-chavez-sadden-shock-chicagos-latino-community" target="_blank" >There are now calls to recast how he is remembered</a>. In Chicago, Chavez is honored with the school name, a plaque at the Haymarket Memorial in the West Loop, and murals located from Southport to Little Village.</p>

Ruddock was born, doctors told his family they didn’t think he would live. He had health problems because his mother was addicted to heroin when she was pregnant.</p><p>Ruddock doesn’t see his upbringing as a sad story, but he does think he became a product of the negative parts of his environment. title: CPS revokes Aspira’s ability to operate charter schools in Chicago in rare move
author: Emmanuel Camarillo
summary: <p>The Chicago Board of Education voted unanimously Thursday to end its contract with the financially troubled Aspira charter network — the only time the school district has revoked a charter in the middle of the school year.</p><p>The charter will officially become inactive on April 4 and students will not be able to enroll at an Aspira school for next year.</p><p>Aspira’s two high schools started the school year with about 600 students, but the campuses are being emptied out. <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/2026/03/05/aspira-will-soon-have-no-teachers-or-money-cps-is-still-struggling-to-close-it" target="_blank" ><u>Aspira’s leaders said the organization didn’t have enough money</u></a> to continue operating through the end of the school year, while the district said state law forbade it from <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/2025/11/25/cps-to-help-aspira-make-payroll-but-charter-operators-financial-woes-remain" target="_blank" ><u>continuing to float Aspira as much cash</u></a> as it needed.</p><p>Board members did not comment before they canceled Aspira’s contract, but in the past, several said <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/2025/11/19/chicago-public-schools-aspira-charter-network-finances-cps-investigation" target="_blank" ><u>Aspira’s poor financial management</u></a> necessitated the closure. They also said they felt terrible about the students having to transition midyear.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/2026/03/19/former-aspira-students-try-to-adapt-after-troubled-charter-operator-closes-schools-midyear" >Former Aspira students try to adapt after troubled charter operator closes schools midyear</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>The last time the school board took the dramatic action of revoking a charter contract <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/2019/12/11/chicago-board-of-education-votes-to-close-two-charter-schools" target="_blank" ><u>was in December 2019</u></a>, though there have been other instances in which the school board did not renew a charter contract, or a charter operator decided to walk away. Over the past 10 years, more than 20 privately run charter or contract schools have closed in Chicago.</p><p>CPS interim CEO/Supt. Macquline King said she and her staff did not recommend Aspira’s charter revocation lightly.</p><p>“It follows a period of intensive monitoring of Aspira’s financial and operational stability, which CPS has determined to be severely lacking,” she told the board before the vote. “Despite our district providing $2.55 million in emergency financial advances to help maintain school operations, Aspira leadership has failed to provide a verified plan to fund operations through the remainder of the school year.”</p><p>Jen Conant, who works with unionized teachers at the Chicago Teachers Union, said at a news conference ahead of the board meeting that she hoped “today’s vote sends a clear signal that charter operators cannot play fast and loose with their money or with students' lives” and that “it helps us keep students from ever facing a crisis like this again.”</p><p>Aspira CEO Edgar Lopez told WBEZ on Wednesday that he was already talking to attorneys about next steps if the board went ahead with the revocation. He thinks he has a case because, he said, the school district provides charter schools less funding than they are supposed to receive under state law.</p><p>He was angry and distraught over the situation. He said he believes the vote to revoke Aspira’s charter was taken on behalf of the Chicago Teachers Union, which he argues controls the school board. The CTU represents Aspira’s school staff but has long been critical of publicly funded, privately run schools.</p><p>Lopez and other charter leaders have accused CPS of underfunding charter schools, and Lopez believes the loss of Aspira’s charter is retaliation for his speaking out about the issue.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Aspira of Illinois CEO Edgar Lopez addresses school board members at the Feb. 26 monthly meeting in an attempt to save the charter school network. </p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Talia Sprague/For the Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>A legal battle might also ensue over Aspira’s school buildings. One of the two schools is in a modern, four-story building in Avondale. The other is in an older building that was renovated when Aspira put a school there.</p><p>Charter contracts say “any property or assets of the Charter School purchased with public funds for the operations of the Charter School … shall be returned to the Board, at no cost to the Board.”</p><p>When the school district <a class="Link" href="https://www.cpsboe.org/content/documents/march_19_2026_public_agenda_to_post.pdf" target="_blank" >laid out its rationale</a> for revoking the charter, officials noted that on Jan. 28, they issued an inquiry to Aspira about property transfers and “received information that ASPIRA transferred two of its properties to a newly created business entity” called the Aspira Illinois Foundation.</p><p>CPS asked Aspira for more details, but it is unclear if the district ever received the financial records it was seeking. CPS officials said in a statement that “accounting for all property and assets during wind-down is critical to protecting the Board’s interests and rights under the agreement.”</p><p>Lopez told WBEZ that the two properties transferred did not include Aspira’s schools. But he also said that he believes Aspira can retain those buildings as long as they use them for programs.</p><p>“This is not going to be turned into a for-profit usage in the buildings. That's not our intent, and it’s never going to happen,” Lopez said. “We're working on different plans, but CPS, they just want to kill us.”</p><p>Aspira of Illinois, the umbrella organization that includes the charter network, <a class="Link" href="https://aspirail.org/who-we-are/" target="_blank" >has been in operation for nearly 60 years</a>, and has some youth programming separate from the school. Aspira also runs an alternative school through a CPS contract with the organization Youth Connection Charter School. CPS says YCCS plans to keep the alternative school open at least through the end of the school year.</p><p>CPS and Aspira blame each other for the charter network’s downfall. CPS says that Aspira created budgets based on unrealistic enrollment projections, while Lopez says CPS’ student assignment system directed students away from charter schools like his. He said underfunding and low enrollment made the schools difficult to operate.</p><p>Conant of the CTU said the charter network’s mismanagement has <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/2026/02/26/cps-to-shut-down-financially-distressed-aspira-campuses-scattering-students-to-new-schools" target="_blank" ><u>produced “chaos” for students and families</u></a>.</p><p>“Given the irresponsible management we have seen this year, and the cost to students' education, the district has no choice but to revoke their charter,” Conant said.</p><p>Conant applauded the district for helping students find new schools. Fewer than 50 students remain at the two closing Aspira schools, she added, and the operator has sent the CTU letters indicating they will have no staff or students after April 3. She said the district should now focus on making sure teachers can also join their students.</p>

title: Former Aspira students try to adapt after troubled charter operator closes schools midyear
author: Sarah Karp | WBEZ
summary: <p>Efrain Aguirre got lost as he tried to find his classes in Schurz High School’s massive brown-brick building that has four floors and takes up an entire city block.</p><p>But he felt encouraged when Schurz students graciously pointed him in the right direction. That kindness gave him “a little confidence” that he would eventually feel okay about going to school there.</p><p>It has only been a week since the junior left Aspira Business & Finance High School, one of two schools run by the financially distressed Aspira charter network that is in the process of an unprecedented midyear school closing.</p><p>At a welcoming event in Schurz’s gym on Wednesday, Efrain said he still felt “questionable” and “worried” about transferring to the neighborhood high school in Irving Park on the city’s Northwest Side.</p><p>“I am pretty new here and I just started talking to people to see if I could find friends,” said the skinny teenager wearing a blue sweatshirt, who was the only one from his friend group to enroll in Schurz.</p><div class="Enhancement" class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Transfer students often find Schurz High School’s large brick building difficult to navigate. The school’s principal noted that as she asked her students to welcome former Aspira students to their campus.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Anthony Vazquez/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>As Aspira closes its schools, Chicago Public Schools faces some important questions. Among them: Can it successfully usher some 570 teenagers to new schools in March without some students falling through the cracks? And can it do anything now to make sure students at other privately run schools with financial issues don’t experience a similar kind of disruption?</p><p>CPS officials have promised to provide bus cards, tutoring and mental health support to Aspira students and to waive their student fees. The district is also putting a transition coordinator at schools that take in a lot of students, like Schurz.</p><p>Conrad Timbers-Ausar, the interim chief of the CPS department that oversees charters, said district staff are reaching out to each Aspira student to make sure they get into a school “that meets their individual needs.” He said some students are still “maybe not sure where they want to go.”</p><p>Over the past two weeks, more than 540 students left Aspira schools. About 30 students were still officially enrolled as of Thursday at Aspira’s two campuses.</p><p>Several publicly funded, privately run schools in Chicago have closed in recent years. But Aspira’s wind-down is different from these other schools, almost all of which closed in the summer, allowing students to transfer at the start of a new school year, when other new students are showing up, too.</p><p>Another difference: Aspira leaders initially fought their closure and sent mixed messages to families about whether they should find new schools, making the transition even harder for some students.</p><h3><b>Charter trouble gives neighborhood high school a boost</b></h3><p>Aspira’s financial troubles have been apparent for months. CEO Edgar Lopez announced in November that the charter network did not have enough money to make it through the school year. The district provided cash advances this fall, but last month CPS officials said the amount Aspira needed was beyond what they could legally provide.</p><p>Before Aspira students were officially told to transfer, some said they were nervous to attend a nearby high school, like Schurz, because they’d heard about safety issues.</p><p>Lopez says some students have already come back to Aspira, complaining about the neighborhood schools they transferred into. He said he was concerned that CPS encouraged students to attend four “underperforming neighborhood schools.” Now he’s urging his former students to attend Intrinsic Schools’ Belmont campus, a nearby charter that’s one of the higher performing schools in the area.</p><p>But for Schurz and other neighborhood high schools, the closing of Aspira’s campuses represents an opportunity. They have seen enrollment declines for two decades as families have had fewer children, moved out of the city, or chosen to send their children to other schools. Taking in lots of students midyear could end up stabilizing their enrollment.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a She called an all-school virtual meeting and hosted a welcoming fair to help with the transition.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Anthony Vazquez/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Twenty-five years ago, Schurz’s hulking building was almost at capacity with more than 2,500 students. But it started this school year with about 1,000.</p><p>Schurz’s principal, Heidy Moran, knew it was important to take extra steps to welcome her new students.</p><p>Once it became clear that Aspira’s schools were shutting down, Moran had the entire student body log into the Google Meet app for a virtual town hall. </p><p>“She gave this talk to everybody, saying, ‘Listen, Schurz is a place where we welcomed you,” recounted Praise Lee, who coordinates the school’s International Baccalaureate program. “‘Think back to the first time that you were at our school, either as a freshman or as a transfer student, and what did that feel like for you? What we want to do is open our hearts and our doors to people who need a place to study.’”</p><p>Lee says that message set the tone as more than 200 Aspira students enrolled at Schurz in the three weeks that followed.</p><p>“We are a little bit shell shocked by it, but also it energized us,” Lee said.</p><p>Moran previously taught at a charter elementary school on the Far South Side, a job she loved.</p><p>But she says being at a neighborhood school has “totally transformed her thinking.” She now sees that district-run schools are chock-full of opportunities and that negative reputations can stick to neighborhood schools after they are no longer true.</p><h3><b>How Schurz students are welcoming classmates from Aspira</b></h3><p>Before the Aspira students enrolled, Moran interviewed other students who previously transferred into Schurz. She said they told her that they were “overwhelmed by the size of the building” and, while the teachers were welcoming, the students were “friendly, but not all that open.” That informed what she said title: Mayor Johnson signals support for letting CPS students take a day off to push for school funding
author: Fran Spielman
summary: <p>Mayor Brandon Johnson on Monday hinted strongly that he supports the Chicago Teachers Union’s call to officially sanction a one-day strike on May 1 that would allow students at Chicago Public Schools to miss a day of classes to make their case for increased school funding.</p><p>Johnson is a former middle school teacher and paid organizer for the CTU — whose mayoral campaign was buoyed by $5.6 million in campaign contributions and hundreds of foot soldiers provided by the CTU and its affiliates.</p><p>His decision to declare a record $1 billion tax increment financing surplus helped to rescue CPS and bankroll the new teachers contract.</p><p>Now the teachers union wants the mayor and CPS's hybrid school board still narrowly controlled by Johnson’s appointees to essentially sanction May 1 as a school holiday, which would allow students to participate in a “no school, no work, no shopping” day.</p><p>Appearing Monday on WBEZ-FM Radio’s “Ask the Mayor” program, Johnson said his longstanding push to tax major corporations and the wealthy Chicagoans to bolster school funding has so far gone nowhere — and it’s time to push the envelope by turning talk into protest action.</p><p>"People all over the country are tired. Working people have had to bear the weight of a sluggish economy while the ultra-rich continue to get richer. Our schools are woefully underfunded… People want more investment in our public transportation system,” the mayor said. “All of that requires a push from working people to challenge elected leaders.”</p><p>WBEZ host Sasha-Ann Simons noted that CPS students already will be off Tuesday and Wednesday this week, and will be off all next week for spring break and again on April 3.</p><p>Johnson said he's aware of that, but argued that CPS parents also "want their schools to be fully-funded." </p><p>“If we just believe that we can just sit on our hands and just hope and wish, that clearly has not worked. I’ve called for taxing corporations and I’ve had other elected leaders fight me who are also Democrats," he said.</p><p>Johnson said Rev. Jesse Jackson, the civil rights icon who died last month at the age of 84, would never have achieved all that he did without “direct action and organizing.” He “literally had to protest to ensure that we have a right to vote,” a right that is now under threat, the mayor said.</p><p>“We are experiencing unprecedented levels of attack [on] the gains that our ancestors made. And if we believe for one minute that the way in which we’re gonna receive our God-given rights our is by just simply asking questions or having town halls — absent taking it to the streets — we are missing the moment,” the mayor said. “We have to push… government to do right by working people. And that will require protest.”</p><p>Ald. Jeanette Taylor (20th), Johnson’s handpicked chair of the City Council’s Education Committee, has two grandchildren who attend Chicago Public Schools. Taylor said she does not believe the mayor should sanction students to skip classes, unless they learn something from it.</p><p>“Are they going down to Springfield? Are they coming down to City Hall? What work is gonna be done? There needs to be something else other than just taking a day off. I want young people to understand them taking the day off. Are we teaching them about May Day? Are we teaching them about workers rights? Are we teaching them to advocate in Springfield for themselves? What comes with it?” Taylor said.</p><p>"It has to be a day of action. Don’t ask me to let my kids take a day off of school so they can sit at home, because we know what they’re gonna do at home. They’re gonna be on the internet. They’re gonna be doing everything but what they’re supposed to be doing.”</p><p>The resolution approved by the CTU’s 730-member House of Delegates last week calls for CPS to join a national movement embracing <a class="Link" href="https://maydaystrong.org/" target="_blank" >a day of “no school, no work, no shopping</a>.” Participants plan to call for higher taxes on the wealthy, better-funded schools, protections for immigrants and other reforms.</p><p>Union leaders cited several reasons for participating, including to demand that ICE gets “out of our cities,” referring to the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agency, and to push to “tax the rich to support our schools and vital services,” according to the resolution. It also says public education is facing attacks from “MAGA politicians” who support the policies of President Donald Trump and “corporate interests."</p><p>The union wants members and students to use the day to take part in “age-appropriate” civic education, labor history programming, voter registration and know-your-rights training, as well as rallies and marches.</p>

title: Local school council elections are upon us — Wednesday — a day after the Illinois primary
author: Letters to the Editor
summary: <p>The Illinois primary will be held Tuesday. The next day is another important day for Chicago residents to vote. That day, please visit your local school to vote in your local school council election.</p><p>Parents, learn about the candidates, and their priorities and visions. Community members, you can vote even if you’re not a parent. Support candidates who reflect what you care about in public education.</p><p>Chicago is world-famous for our politics — perhaps not always in a good way. But for many of our neighbors, LSC elections fly under the radar. They date back to the late 1980s, when then-Mayor Harold Washington led an effort to better share power among staff, families and neighborhoods in schools.</p><p>Every CPS school has an LSC, and every two years, Chicago undertakes one of the largest local elections in the country, where parents, staff, community members and students vote for representatives.</p><p>We are leaders of our neighborhood elementary school’s LSC. Working together, we are building a place where children thrive.</p><p>LSCs are elected bodies — mini school boards made up of parents, teachers, neighbors and students. They do not run schools directly but have real power and responsibility. LSCs vote on school improvement plans, approve school budgets, and evaluate or hire principals. They provide rare spaces to hear one another’s perspectives and strengthen school communities.</p><p>Coming out of the pandemic, we saw that children urgently needed support both emotionally and academically. We made these priorities in our school’s improvement plan, and voted to invest in social-emotional learning and academic intervention to help students recover.</p><p>Recently, student musicians performed a Women’s History Month rock show; eighth graders held a debate about the death penalty in literature class; and students stayed after school to rehearse for the spring play.</p><p>These came from LSC decisions to invest in after-school programs, arts positions, bilingual education and bringing parent mentors into classrooms.</p><p>No matter where you live in Chicago, you have a neighborhood school, and that means you have an LSC. Make sure you vote March 18!</p><p><i>Ben Dieterich, local school council chair, and Seth Lavin, principal, Brentano Math & Science Academy</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-bc0000" name="module-bc0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>Give us your take</h3><br>Send letters to the editor to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. To be considered for publication, letters must include your full name, your neighborhood or hometown and a phone number for verification purposes. Letters should be a maximum of approximately 375 words.</div> </div><p></p><h3><b>Nonviolence needs to be political ideal everywhere</b></h3><p>Democracy is in decline across the globe. Extremism is rising, strongman politics is gaining appeal, and disagreements too often harden into hatred. The warning signs are everywhere.</p><p>This moment calls us back to the moral tradition shared by Mahatma Gandhi, Martin Luther King Jr. and the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/2026/03/06/rev-jesse-jackson-chicago-service-house-of-hope-pullman-neighborhood-barack-obama-jb-pritzker" >Rev. Jesse Jackson</a> — a lineage rooted in the power of disciplined nonviolence. Gandhi called his philosophy <a class="Link" href="https://www.britannica.com/topic/satyagraha-philosophy" target="_blank" >Satyagraha</a>, or truth-force: the belief that moral courage and collective action can confront injustice without reproducing cycles of violence.</p><p>Gandhi’s ideas did not remain confined to India. They helped shape the American Civil Rights Movement. King studied Gandhi’s strategy carefully and <a class="Link" href="https://kinginstitute.stanford.edu/india-trip" target="_blank" >visited India in 1959</a>, later calling him <a class="Link" href="https://www.politico.com/story/2013/03/mahatma-gandhis-lightguided-martin-luther-king-jr-088581" target="_blank" >“the guiding light of our technique of nonviolent social change.”</a></p><p>Chicago became an important center of that tradition. For decades, Jackson — King’s protégé — expanded the practice of nonviolence beyond protest. Through coalition-building and economic justice advocacy, Jackson showed that love and democracy must be defended in the streets and within institutions of power.</p><p>Today, the stakes are global. Even in India, the land Gandhi helped liberate, extremist ideologies have gained ground. Around the world, including in the U.S., democratic norms are being tested by intolerance, disinformation and the influence of political funding.</p><p>Chicago's <a class="Link" href="https://www.sacreddemocracy.org/" target="_blank" >South Asian American Coalition to Renew Democracy Acts</a>, or SACRED Acts, has taken up this charge locally. As part of the Season for Nonviolence, it launched a pledge urging candidates and elected officials to reject financial support from organizations tied to extremist, caste-supremacist or hate-based ideologies.</p><p>At a public news conference at which I delivered the keynote, 50-plus local leaders joined my call to reject funding from anti-democratic groups like the <a class="Link" href="https://www.npr.org/2019/05/03/706808616/the-powerful-group-shaping-the-rise-of-hindu-nationalism-in-india" target="_blank" >Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh</a>, a right-wing paramilitary group that planned the assassination of my great-grandfather. While I feel disappointment at prominent leaders who did not sign on, those who did sign on reaffirmed their commitment to expose money trails that undermine democratic values — whether in India or the U.S.</p><p>This effort reflects the same moral lineage that shaped Gandhi, King and Jackson: the belief that nonviolence is not only a personal ethic but a public responsibility. Nonviolence or nonexistence is not merely a slogan. It is a choice about the kind of democracy we will build — and whether we will defend it together.</p><p><i>Tushar Gandhi, founder, Mahatma Gandhi Foundation, Mumbai, India</i></p><h3>‘Nothing left to target’</h3><p>Dear President Trump: I heard on CNN last week that you said, via <a class="Link" href="https://www.axios.com/2026/03/11/trump-iran-war-end-withdrawal" target="_blank" >Axios</a>, there was "practically nothing left" to target in Iran.</p><p>When I was in Vietnam in 1969, at age 19, I suggested to our top sergeant the way to end the war was to bomb the country, grid square by grid square, until there would be nothing left to target.</p><p>We could have used you to end that war, six years before it actually ended. Oh, I forgot: bone spurs. Five cases of them. It must have been tough to live with them.</p><p><i>Calogero Lombardo, Old Irving Park</i></p>

title: CPS investigating Taft High School employee’s ‘inappropriate’ interactions with students
author: Kade Heather
summary: <p>The Chicago Public Schools’ inspector general’s office has launched an investigation into an employee at a Norwood Park neighborhood high school.</p><p>A staff member at William Howard Taft High School, 6530 W. Bryn Mawr Ave., has been accused of engaging “inappropriately with students,” according to a notice obtained by the Sun-Times. Taft Principal Ryan Glowacz sent the notice to students’ families Wednesday afternoon.</p><p>The employee has been removed from the school while the CPS inspector general’s office investigates, the notice said.</p><p>A final determination whether to reinstate the staff member will be made based on information learned during the investigation, Glowacz said.</p><p>“Please know that we are taking this situation seriously, and we remain committed to providing your children with a safe, positive learning environment where they can reach their full potential,” Glowacz said. “While I am unable to discuss details regarding the investigation, I am always available to discuss steps the district takes to keep students safe and matters related to your child.”</p>

title: Threat deemed 'non credible' at Lane Tech, school says
author: Sun-Times Wire
summary: <p>A potential threat called in to Lane Tech College Prep that prompted visits from the police and fire departments has been deemed 'non-credible' and no students or staff are in any danger, the school said. </p><p>At 1:25 p.m. firefighters were called to the school, 2501 W. Addison St., for a call about an 'unknown object,' said Chicago Fire Department spokesperson Larry Merritt. A Level 1 hazardous materials call for the object was "secured" at 1:44 p.m., he added.</p><p>Merritt said he didn't know why the object was suspicious.</p><p>The school was placed on soft lockdown after receiving a phone call from an unknown source that included a potential threat to our school, Lane Tech principal Edwina Thompson said in a letter sent to parents and guardians. </p><p>Police later determined the potential threat was "non-credible, Thompson said in the statement. </p><p>"There is no safety threat to our school, and everyone is safe. All after-school activities are expected to proceed as planned."</p><p>Chicago police had no further details immediately. </p><p>According to police radio transmissions, the call happened during sixth period, a "soft lockdown" was put in place, and some of the students were moved to another building.</p><p>A Chicago police officer on the scene reported to an OEMC dispatcher they were detaining someone after a backpack was found in the men's washroom on the second floor of the school. </p><p>“I have him in my custody,’’ the officer told the dispatcher. “There’s a backpack…I’ve not heard any noises or sounds from the backpack.”</p><p>A Chicago Public Schools representative did not immediately respond to a request for comment.</p><p><i>This is a developing story. Check back for updates.</i></p>

title: Trinity dancers delight as St. Patrick's Day nears
author: Sun-Times staff

title: CPS Board names 3 finalists to lead district: Interim CEO King, former NYC, East Baton Rouge schools chiefs
author: Emmanuel Camarillo
summary: <p>The Chicago Board of Education announced three finalists to run the school district Friday.</p><p>One surprising name on the list: Macquline King, who has been serving as interim leader of Chicago Public Schools since June, after originally being told she was not in the running.</p><p>She joins Meisha Porter, the first Black woman to lead New York City’s school system, and Sito Narcisse, a former superintendent of Louisiana’s East Baton Rouge Parish schools and chief of secondary schools in the District of Columbia. Narcisse is the son of Haitian immigrants.</p><p>Next week, the finalists will meet with Mayor Brandon Johnson and will be interviewed by a panel of 15 that includes students, parents, teachers and community members.</p><p>The announcement comes after a months-long search process that encountered several hiccups.</p><p>Originally, school board members did not plan to make the names of the finalists public because the search firm they hired said that would discourage candidates from applying. But in November, Porter and another candidate's name became public, and that candidate dropped out of contention.</p><p>At that point, the search was re-opened and board members conducted a new round of interviews.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-c80000" name="image-c80000"></a> In Chicago, only 35% of households that included adults in this age group were working at least 20 hours per week, according to a Chicago Sun-Times and WBEZ analysis of data from the U.S. Census 2024 American Community Survey.</p><p><b>The stakes</b>: The new requirements call for people to work or volunteer 80 hours a month, which translates to an average four hours per weekday. The rules also expanded to include veterans and parents whose youngest child is 14 years or older. If SNAP recipients don’t meet the rules or get an exemption by May, they will begin losing benefits.</p><p><b>Uphill battles</b>: Older people who have been out of the workforce might find it harder to compete for jobs, especially because of continuing ageism, advocates say. This group also often spends time looking after relatives, making it harder to meet the 80 hours each month. In response, community groups across Chicago are expanding volunteer opportunities.</p><p><a class="Link" target="_blank" >How Quinn Chapel AME put its faith in action</a></h3><h5>By <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-wtriuhd-tlkjhhnv-q/" target="_blank" >Nicole Jeanine Johnson</a></h5><p><b>Community heart</b>: By the 1840s, free Blacks flocked to Chicago to steer clear of slavery. Some of them started Quinn Chapel AME, the city’s first Black church, and its physical building served as a beacon for freedom seekers. As the law closed free Blacks off from public society, the church became the center of the community. It was where people learned to read, engaged in debate club, and had women’s Bible study and singing classes.</p><p><b>Underground Railroad station</b>: Those who led Quinn Chapel’s emancipation work were among the city’s Black elite — leaders in the business community and in politics. But the veil of class, wealth and mixed ancestry didn't fool church members into thinking they couldn’t be returned to slavery or taken into bondage for the first time. The chapel's location along the Chicago River, with close proximity to Lake Michigan, made it a strategic station on the Underground Railroad.</p><p><b>Living history</b>: Inside the church is a massive organ purchased from the 1893 World’s Columbian Exposition German pavilion. Members at the time held the first ever June Rose benefit concert to pay for the instrument. Since then, Quinn Chapel has hosted the concerts for more than 130 years. "It’s kind of a homecoming for everybody," Senior Pastor Troy Venning said.</p><p><a class="Link" title: High school students ace early voting program
author: Letters to the Editor
summary: <p>High school students made voting history in suburban Cook County, and they did it in a single day.</p><p>Through the clerk’s new "Defenders of DA'mocracy" High School Early Voting Program, student-run early voting sites inside 24 suburban high schools recorded 1,136 ballots cast on Feb. 26. To put that in perspective, that single-day total surpassed the 1,021 ballots cast during the first seven days of early voting at our initial countywide locations.</p><p>This is more than a milestone — it is proof that when we bring civic engagement directly to young people, they respond.</p><p>Developed in partnership with the Chicago Bears, this first-of-its-kind initiative placed fully operational early voting sites inside participating high schools. More than 125 trained and certified student election judges administered official polling locations under the supervision of the Cook County clerk’s office. They handled voter check-in, secured ballots, operated voting equipment and followed the same strict chain-of-custody and security protocols used at every polling place across suburban Cook County.</p><p>This was not a simulation. It was democracy in action.</p><p>Research shows that when young people participate in their first eligible election, they are far more likely to remain engaged for years to come. By bringing early voting directly into high schools, we are removing barriers, building confidence and fostering lifelong civic participation at a formative moment.</p><p>The energy inside these schools was inspiring. Students were not only casting ballots, they were also leading, administering and safeguarding the democratic process. That is an investment in the future of our community that will pay dividends for years to come.</p><p>Expanded early voting continues across suburban Cook County, with <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/03/01/early-voting-chicago-suburbs" >55 locations</a> open ahead of Tuesday's gubernatorial primary election. I encourage all eligible voters to take advantage of this opportunity and make their voices heard.</p><p>Democracy is strongest when participation is broad, inclusive and accessible — and our students have shown us exactly what that looks like.</p><p><i>Monica Gordon, Cook County clerk</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-500000" name="module-500000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>Give us your take</h3><br>Send letters to the editor to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. To be considered for publication, letters must include your full name, your neighborhood or hometown and a phone number for verification purposes. Letters should be a maximum of approximately 375 words.</div> </div><p></p><h3>Energy engagement </h3><p>Thank you for the two articles on important energy issues in the March 6 Sun-Times. The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/money/2026/03/04/chicago-construction-clayco-solar-power-energy-business" >article </a>by Amy Yee — "Chicago-based construction firm Clayco launches solar energy business" — underlines the need for vastly more use of solar, as well as wind and geothermal power — all alternative power sources.</p><p>But another <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/springfield/2026/03/04/alternative-energy-suppliers-electricity-bills-reform-legislation" >article</a> in the same paper — "For alternative energy supplier customers who routinely overpay, proposed reforms could provide some help" — confuses the issue by calling some different providers "alternatives" to the traditional suppliers. These different providers including North American Power, may or may not supply energy from alternative sources. The difference is important, because alternative sources can provide energy without climate change, and for less. </p><p><i>Ann Boisclair, Glen Ellyn</i><br></p>

title: CTU plans to join May 1 ‘no school, no work’ day of action, wants classes canceled
author: Emmanuel Camarillo
summary: <p>The Chicago Teachers Union intends to launch what amounts to a one-day strike on May 1 and is asking the mayor and school board for their official support so students can miss school to participate.</p><p>On Wednesday the union’s 730-member House of Delegates <a class="Link" href="https://www.ctulocal1.org/posts/mayday-resolution/?link_id=2&can_id=17ebc6e1a278c81ea80307c4c5703485&source=email-ctu-members-vote-to-join-may-1st-no-school-no-work-no-shopping-day-of-civic-action&email_referrer=email_3140500&email_subject=ctu-members-vote-to-join-may-1st-no-school-no-work-no-shopping-day-of-civic-action" target="_blank" ><u>approved a resolution</u></a> to join a national movement <a class="Link" href="https://maydaystrong.org/" target="_blank" >calling for a day of “no school, no work, no shopping</a>.” Participants plan to call for higher taxes on the wealthy, better-funded schools, protections for immigrants and other reforms.</p><p>Union leaders cited several reasons for participating, including to “demand ICE out of our cities,” referring to the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agency, and “tax the rich to support our schools and vital services,” according to the resolution. It also says public education is facing attacks from “MAGA politicians” who support the policies of President Donald Trump and “corporate interests.”</p><p>That day, the union wants members and students to take part in “age-appropriate” civic education, labor history programming, voter registration and know-your-rights training, as well as rallies and marches.</p><p>“Teaching our students what civic action looks like requires more than textbooks when the President sends federal agents to occupy our cities and the Governor chooses to continue giving tax breaks to billionaires instead of giving our students the school day they deserve,” CTU Vice President Jackson Potter said in a statement.</p><p>The union wants Mayor Brandon Johnson and the school board to make May 1 “an official day of action,” saying the mayor can draw <a class="Link" href="https://www.ilga.gov/Documents/legislation/ilcs/documents/010500050K26-1.htm" target="_blank" ><u>upon a state law</u></a> that allows middle and high school students one excused absence per year to attend a “civic event.”</p><p>CTU encouraged its members to <a class="Link" href="https://actionnetwork.org/petitions/may-day-civic-action-day/?link_id=2&can_id=17ebc6e1a278c81ea80307c4c5703485&source=email-may-1st-no-work-no-school-no-shopping-teletownhall-monday-at-6-pm-for-more-2&email_referrer=email_3140628&email_subject=may-1st-no-work-no-school-no-shopping&&" target="_blank" ><u>sign a petition calling for the mayor</u></a> to take action.</p><p>In a statement, Johnson said he would “work with our partners at CPS and in our school communities to find solutions which ensure there is no loss of instruction time.”</p><p>But he indicated support for the broader movement, saying the effort to organize on May 1 “offers working people across the country the opportunity to make their voice heard through direct action.”</p><p>Chicago Public Schools didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.</p><p>Kevin Moore, a CTU member and social studies teacher at George Washington High School, said it's important for the union to participate in the action because “public education is under attack” and “we shouldn't stand for that.”</p><p>Moore added that though students may not be in school that day, they will still learn something.</p><p>“We’re teaching our students how to use their voice,” Moore said. “We're teaching our students that they have a very powerful role in defending democracy and that they have a role in building the country that we need, in the future they deserve.”</p><p>The CTU has engaged in similar one-day actions before. <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/chicago/2016/04/01/chicago-teachers-stage-rare-1-day-strike" target="_blank" ><u>In 2016, teachers staged a rare one-day strike</u></a> in support of higher wages and more state funding. That action led CPS to cancel school for the day and set up contingency sites where parents who needed to work could drop off their children. <a class="Link" href="https://www.chicagoreporter.com/liveblog-april-1-ctu-strike/" target="_blank" ><u>CPS filed a charge</u></a> with the Illinois Educational Labor Relations Board alleging the strike was illegal.</p><p>Staging actions on International Workers’ Day, also known as May Day, has a long history. The holiday’s origins date back to Chicago’s Haymarket Affair of 1886, <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/reset-with-sasha-ann-simons/2023/05/01/may-day-marks-chicagos-history-of-fighting-for-workers-rights" target="_blank" ><u>a workers’ rights strike</u></a> where several demonstrators, police and civilians died. In the mid-2000s, hundreds of thousands of people participated in <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/2008/04/30/may-day-leaders-predict-strong-march" target="_blank" ><u>May Day marches to support immigrant rights.</u></a></p><p>On May 1 last year, the CTU participated in rallies and marches, too. Though it was a regular school day for students, the union said about <a class="Link" href="https://www.ctulocal1.org/posts/may-day-2025-history-made-lets-keep-it-going/" target="_blank" ><u>500 students participated in the march.</u></a></p>

title: CPS should work to prevent future attendance drops due to immigration enforcement, community groups say
author: Sarah Karp | WBEZ
summary: <p>A coalition of community groups and a parent advocacy organization are urging Chicago Public Schools to take steps now to prevent attendance declines should there be another surge in federal immigration enforcement.</p><p>Among the things they are asking for: More frequent updates about attendance trends and designated safe spaces where students and parents can retreat should they encounter a threat while going to or from school.</p><p>“So much was needed for our families that we were not prepared for,” said Ana Lorenzana of the Northwest Center in Belmont Cragin, who spoke Wednesday during a virtual briefing on <a class="Link" href="https://kidsfirstchicago.org/assets/miscellaneous/2026-K1C-Safe-Passage-report-v5.pdf" target="_blank" ><u>a report that her organization and several others worked to produce</u></a>.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2026/03/10/chicago-immigration-deport-trump-noem-bovino-midway-blitz" target="_blank" ><u>It is unclear whether President Donald Trump</u></a> will ramp up the number of agents in Chicago and employ the kind of aggressive tactics that ravaged immigrant communities with fear this past fall. For now, there are no signs of a spring surge, as these tactics are under scrutiny and top officials, including U.S. Border Patrol Cmdr. Gregory Bovino, are no longer in their positions.</p><p>But if it does happen, the school system needs to be ready, unlike in the fall when the response was, according to the report, “uneven, fragile, and unsustainable.”</p><p>“The good news is that we have time to prepare,”said Daniel Anello, chief executive director of the parent advocacy organization Kids First Chicago, which spearheaded the report. “I think the bad news is we don't have too much time to prepare, given where we are, and we really need to get organized.”</p><p>Kids First Chicago partnered with the <a class="Link" href="https://authenticengagement.info/" target="_blank" ><u>Coalition for Authentic Community Engagement</u></a>, a group that includes the pastors of prominent Black churches and organizations that serve or represent many of the city’s immigrant communities, including Chinese Americans and Middle Eastern refugees.</p><p>CPS officials said they appreciate the report’s focus on collaboration and will evaluate its recommendations.</p><p>“We remain committed to working alongside all partners to strengthen our practices and ensure educators and students can thrive in a secure environment,” a CPS spokesperson wrote in a statement.</p><p>While CPS has regularly stated that overall attendance did not suffer much this fall, the report’s authors reached a conclusion similar to <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/2025/12/02/as-immigration-agents-swept-chicago-this-fall-communities-stepped-in-to-get-kids-to-school-safely" target="_blank" ><u>a WBEZ and Sun-Times analysis earlier this school year</u></a>: There were spikes in absenteeism on particular days and weeks.</p><p>Higher-than-usual absenteeism among English Language Learners was a particular problem, the group found. In the seventh week of school, 3,000 more English Language Learners stayed home, compared to previous years, they estimated.</p><p>Marlon Henriquez, principal of Gunsaulus Scholastic Academy, a magnet school in the Southwest Side neighborhood of Brighton Park, said once the federal enforcement activity died down, attendance bounced back at the elementary school.</p><p>“Our families want to come to school,” he said. “That is very clear.”</p><p>But attendance among high school students who are English Language Learners has not fully rebounded, Anello said. He said “there’s more work to be done” to re-engage those students.</p><p>The report lays out several recommendations, including prioritizing getting support to communities where there has been a lot of immigration enforcement and, consequently, high absenteeism.</p><p>In these communities especially, the report calls for CPS to publish weekly attendance reports so issues are spotted more quickly.</p><p>The report’s authors say principals and other top staff should get <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/immigration/2025/09/05/volunteers-on-ice-patrol-in-chicagos-pilsen-neighborhood-looking-for-agents" target="_blank" ><u>rapid response training</u></a> and schools should have an arrival and dismissal team with a designated leader who can make sure a protocol is followed when there are threats of federal agents nearby.</p><p>Kids First and the community groups also want CPS to do more to get students to school. They point out that <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/2025/12/02/as-immigration-agents-swept-chicago-this-fall-communities-stepped-in-to-get-kids-to-school-safely" target="_blank" ><u>communities stepped up this fall</u></a>, providing walking school buses, carpools and neighborhood watches. But they say the district needs a more coordinated approach.</p><p>Henriquez said where he lives on the North Side, a lot of residents came out to keep watch over children as they went to and from school. But Gunsaulus is in an area filled with immigrants and residents who were too scared to stand outside and be those eyes and ears.</p><p>“Getting to school and leaving school, that's something that's out of our sphere of control,” he said. “Having individuals present, opening doors, saying good morning, saying goodbye, being a familiar happy face, would make a huge impact in the community of Gunsaulus.”</p><p>The groups say CPS should undo <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/education/2025/08/13/cps-safe-passage" target="_blank" ><u>recent cuts to the Safe Passage program</u></a>, which posts people on corners to watch students go to and from school, and pilot a transportation program that could be used during surges. That could include working with trusted community organizations to shuttle students to school or expanding bus routes, the report says.</p><p>The groups also suggest that school safety committees made up of teachers and other staff be paired with groups of parents who want to be involved.</p><p>Finally, they want CPS to step up its support for <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/education/2026/02/12/no-recess-lockdowns-less-learning-how-immigration-agents-disrupted-cps-schools-this-fall" target="_blank" ><u>students impacted by federal immigration activity</u></a>. They say CPS should expand mental health services and refer students for food and economic support “so temporary fear does not create long-term academic harm.”</p><p>They also say CPS should make sure students have laptops and a reliable internet connection to allow for some remote learning or tutoring if individual students are facing a real safety risk to come to school in person.</p>

title: Program offering academic and financial support helps City Colleges students earn more, study finds
author: Mary Norkol
summary: <p>When Tiara Davis went back to school in her 30s after having three kids, she wasn’t looking to get involved on campus. She just wanted to “keep my head down and get my degree.”</p><p>But as she progressed at Kennedy-King College in Englewood, one of the City Colleges of Chicago, she met a coordinator with One Million Degrees who encouraged her to apply to the nonprofit’s program. She now credits the support and resources it provided with putting her on track to earn an associate degree in computer science in May.</p><p>Davis had dropped out of college before, and she says without the program, she was bound to do it again. Instead, she is gearing up to pursue a four-year degree.</p><p>“I would have 1,000% stopped,” Davis said. “I was coming for an advanced certificate. I’m leaving with an associate degree, and I’m transferring for my bachelor’s. That was not in the plan at all, but it was due to resources like this that made me see that, ‘Hey, there might be something further.’”</p><p>Community college students like Davis who participate in the Chicago-based One Million Degrees program are more likely to earn their degree and see higher wages after they graduate, a <a class="Link" href="https://urbanlabs.uchicago.edu/attachments/d9eeb8b0705c70888bfee9b528b105ebff45dbde/store/1615ccbb464738d2e041de002be60389613d326a8bf53ddda11f91805858/OMD_Long_Term_White_Paper.pdf" target="_blank" ><u>study released Wednesday</u></a> by the University of Chicago Inclusive Economy Lab found. The effects are even greater if students start getting support early, as they transition from high school to community college.</p><p>Researchers say the findings bolster the case that <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/2019/05/02/has-one-million-degrees-found-the-secret-to-community-college-success" target="_blank" ><u>wraparound supports can improve students’ outcomes</u></a> in the workforce whether they are embedded within a college or offered by an outside organization.</p><p>Funded largely by donations and grants, One Million Degrees partners with City Colleges and often works with first-generation and low-income community college students. Students can apply while they’re in high school or if they’re enrolled in community college.</p><p>Students are then matched with a program coordinator who can connect them to various financial, academic, professional and personal supports. That could be tutoring or help finding child care. The program also provides a $750 to $1,000 stipend annually that full-time students can put toward college costs, like books and transportation, so long as they’re passing their classes and attending required meetings.</p><p>“It really meets students where their needs are and targets the support,” said Kelly Hallberg, who co-authored the study and is the scientific director for the Inclusive Economy Lab.</p><p>The newly released data builds upon <a class="Link" href="https://urbanlabs.uchicago.edu/attachments/89ba899bbb8d94545822ecffb39ae94f2c736345/store/466e7cde4a3f66a7c388d8f39c0ca80efc914f34b85caacb63509f4a4de2/Final_OMD+Working+paper_updated+June+2022.pdf" target="_blank" ><u>research released in 2022</u></a> that showed students were more likely to remain in community college during their first year if they got the wraparound support offered by One Million Degrees.</p><p>Now, longer-term benefits of the program are emerging as students grow older and pursue further education and careers.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div
